nameStory: The 'striped' in this spider's name comes from the distinctive pale lines that run down each side of its body like racing stripes on a car. As a fishing spider, it's named for its remarkable ability to hunt on water surfaces, literally fishing for aquatic insects and small fish by detecting vibrations through the water's surface tension.
description: The Striped Fishing Spider is one of New England's largest spiders, with females reaching an impressive legspan of over 6 centimeters - about the size of your palm! These pale brown hunters are beautifully decorated with light-colored stripes running along their sides and wrapped around their legs like bands. Unlike web-building spiders, these athletic arachnids are active hunters that can actually walk on water and dive beneath the surface when threatened.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for the diagnostic pale stripes running down each side of the brown body, plus lighter bands wrapped around the legs like socks - these markings feel slightly raised to the touch

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Females are notably large with legs that can span over 6 cm when fully extended - about the size of a small child's palm

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Robust, athletic build with long powerful legs and a relatively flat body that feels firm when gently touched - built for surface tension walking

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No web for hunting - instead creates a loose nursery web in vegetation when carrying egg sacs, which feels silky but not sticky

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen near water edges with front legs touching the surface, detecting vibrations - will dive underwater when disturbed, leaving a silvery air bubble coating

habitat: Look for Striped Fishing Spiders along the edges of ponds, slow streams, marshes, and boggy areas throughout New England's lowlands and foothills. They prefer areas with overhanging vegetation like sedges, cattails, or low shrubs where they can easily access both water and shelter. You'll often spot them on wooden docks, fallen logs, or large rocks near water where they can feel vibrations from potential prey.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from overwintering and begin appearing near water sources as temperatures warm. Look for them becoming active on sunny days when water surfaces are calm.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible hunting and mating. Females may be seen carrying large, round egg sacs under their bodies in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Mated females construct nursery webs in vegetation near water where spiderlings emerge. Adults remain active until first hard frost approaches.
seasonality.winter: Juveniles and some adults overwinter under bark, logs, or dense vegetation near water sources, becoming dormant until spring warming.

funFact: When threatened, Striped Fishing Spiders can dive completely underwater and stay submerged for over 30 minutes, breathing from an air bubble trapped in their body hairs - essentially wearing their own personal scuba gear made of silk and air!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with the Dark Fishing Spider, but remember 'light stripes, Striped Spider' - the Striped Fishing Spider has obvious pale stripes while the Dark Fishing Spider is much darker overall with less obvious markings and a more mottled appearance.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name, fishing spiders don't actually fish with lines or webs - they're called 'fishing' spiders because they hunt like a heron, detecting prey movements through water surface vibrations with their sensitive leg tips.
compareHints: Among New England's fishing spiders, the Striped Fishing Spider is distinguished by its pale brown coloration with prominent light stripes, while the Dark Fishing Spider is much darker and larger, and the Six-spotted Fishing Spider has distinctive white spots instead of stripes. The Striped is also generally smaller than its Dark cousin and prefers smaller water bodies like ponds over large lakes or rivers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the striped fishing spider and six-spotted fishing spider which are typically found near water and have more contrasting markings, the dark fishing spider has subtler coloration and lives almost exclusively on trees.
The six-spotted fishing spider is distinguished from its close relative the Dark Fishing Spider by its characteristic six light spots versus the Dark Fishing Spider's white side stripes.
Among New England's fishing spiders, the Banded Fishing Spider is distinguished by its bold, regular light bands across a dark body.
Among New England's fishing spiders, striatus has the most clearly defined striped patterns - other species like the dark fishing spider have more mottled or spotted appearances.

The white-banded fishing spider stands out from its fishing spider relatives by having the most clearly defined white bands - the dark fishing spider has more subdued, mottled markings, while the striped fishing spider shows yellowish stripes rather than bright white bands.
